claim: Pak2 deficiency in mice resulted in embryonic lethality at embryonic day 8.
source: However, Pak2 deficiency resulted in lethality at embryonic day 8 (Hofmann et al., 2004; Arias-Romero and Chernoff, 2008; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites three references (Hofmann et al., 2004; Arias-Romero and Chernoff, 2008; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012) supporting this claim about embryonic lethality.

claim: Over 95% of Pak2 protein was deleted in DP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre or Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: We confirmed that over 95% of Pak2 protein was deleted in DP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre or Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A-C demonstrating protein deletion.

claim: T-cell specific Pak2 deletion using Lck-Cre or Cd4-Cre transgenes resulted in severe T cell lymphopenia.
source: T-cell specific Pak2 deletion using Lck-Cre or Cd4-Cre transgenes resulted in severe T cell lymphopenia (Figure 1D,F,G,J, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data and cell counts shown in multiple figures.

claim: Both CD4 and CD8 peripheral T cells were reduced similarly in Pak2-deficient mice.
source: Both CD4 and CD8 peripheral T cells were reduced similarly.
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D and 1G.

claim: Naïve T cells (CD62LhiCD44low) were almost absent in Pak2-deficient mice.
source: Naïve T cells (CD62LhiCD44low) were almost absent and the few remaining T cells were mostly CD44hi (Figure 1E,H).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 1E and 1H show the absence of naive T cells.

claim: The Lck-Cre transgene is expressed during the DN2 stage.
source: The Lck-Cre transgene is expressed during the DN2 (CD4-CD8-double negative 2) stage (Hennet et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hennet et al., 1995.

claim: The Cd4-Cre transgene is expressed at the DP stage.
source: while the Cd4-Cre transgene is expressed later at the DP stage (Lee et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2001.

claim: Naive T cells generated from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre hematopoietic stem cells had a cell-intrinsic disadvantage in reconstituting the secondary lymphoid organs.
source: Mixed bone marrow chimera (1:1 ratio) experiments revealed that naive T cells generated from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C) or Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre (data not shown) hematopoietic stem cells had a cell-intrinsic disadvantage in reconstituting the secondary lymphoid organs.
evidence: The claim is supported by mixed bone marrow chimera experiments shown in Figure 1I and supplementary figures.

claim: Pak2 is required for generation or homeostasis of peripheral T cells.
source: These results indicate that Pak2 is required for generation or homeostasis of peripheral T cells.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the bone marrow chimera experiments showing cell-intrinsic disadvantage.

claim: Onset of deletion of Pak2 at the DN2 stage in Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice inhibited the transition from the DN to DP stage and subsequent positive selection.
source: Onset of deletion of Pak2 at the DN2 stage in Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice inhibited the transition from the DN to DP stage and subsequent positive selection.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing reduced DP and SP thymocyte numbers in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Total, DP and CD4 and CD8 SP thymocyte numbers were markedly decreased in Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice.
source: Total, DP and CD4 and CD8 SP thymocyte numbers were markedly decreased (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Cell counts shown in Figure 2B demonstrate decreased thymocyte numbers.

claim: DN3 thymocytes in Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice were increased with impaired expression of intracellular TCR β-chain at DN3 but not DN4 stages.
source: DN3 thymocytes in Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice were increased with impaired expression of intracellular TCR β-chain at DN3 but not DN4 stages, suggesting a relative block in development at the checkpoint mediated by the pre-TCR (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2C-D show increased DN3 cells and impaired TCR β-chain expression.

claim: Pak2 deficiency substantially reduced TCRhi CD4 or CD8 SP thymocytes.
source: The majority of TCRhi cells were CD4 or CD8 SP thymocytes in WT mice, but Pak2 deficiency substantially reduced TCRhi CD4 or CD8 SP thymocytes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2E show reduced TCRhi SP thymocytes.

claim: The generation of OTII TCR transgene+ CD4SP thymocytes was greatly reduced in Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice, suggesting defective positive selection.
source: The generation of OTII TCR transgene+ CD4SP thymocytes was greatly reduced, suggesting defective positive selection (Figure 2F–H).
evidence: Data from OTII TCR transgenic mice shown in Figure 2F-H demonstrate reduced CD4SP thymocytes.

claim: Expression of CD5 was markedly lower in DP and CD4SP thymocytes from OTII+;Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice, indicative of lower basal TCR signaling.
source: In addition, the expression of CD5 was markedly lower in DP and CD4SP thymocytes (Figure 2I) with a reduced percentage of post-positive selection cells (data not shown) from OTII+;Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice, indicative of lower basal TCR signaling (Azzam et al., 1998).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 2I show reduced CD5 expression, and the interpretation is supported by citation to Azzam et al., 1998.

claim: Deletion of Pak2 at the DN2 stage markedly impaired T cell development in the thymus by impairing both pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection.
source: Thus, deletion of Pak2 at the DN2 stage markedly impaired T cell development in the thymus by impairing both pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Numbers of DP and CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes were similar in Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice, suggesting generation of CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes was normal.
source: Numbers of DP and CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes were similar, suggesting generation of CD4 and CD8 SP thymocytes was normal in Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Cell counts in Figure 3B show similar numbers of thymocyte subsets.

claim: Expression of CD5, CD69, and CD3 on DP thymocytes were similar between Pak2F/F and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: Expression of CD5, CD69, and CD3 on DP thymocytes were similar between Pak2F/F and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (data not shown).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation but notes data not shown.

claim: The generation of CD4SP thymocytes was markedly reduced in OTII+;Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice, suggesting that Pak2 is required for positive selection.
source: The generation of CD4SP thymocytes was markedly reduced in OTII+;Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 3C–E), suggesting that Pak2 is required for positive selection.
evidence: Data from OTII TCR transgenic mice in Figure 3C-E show reduced CD4SP thymocytes.

claim: CD4SP thymocytes were blocked at the semi-mature stage in Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: Remarkably, CD4SP thymocytes were blocked at the semi-mature stage in Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4A-B show accumulation of semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes.

claim: Expression of CD62L and integrin β7 were reduced in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: Consistent with a defect at this developmental transition, expression of CD62L and integrin β7 were reduced, but CD69 expression remained high in CD4SP thymocytes (Figure 4C, top panels).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4C show altered expression of maturation markers.

claim: CD69 expression remained high in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: Consistent with a defect at this developmental transition, expression of CD62L and integrin β7 were reduced, but CD69 expression remained high in CD4SP thymocytes (Figure 4C, top panels).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4C show maintained high CD69 expression.

claim: Expression of CD3, TCRβ, and CD24 were similar between Pak2F/F and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre CD4SP thymocytes.
source: Expression of CD3, TCRβ, and CD24 were similar between Pak2F/F and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 4C, bottom panels)
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4C show similar expression levels.

claim: A subset of Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre CD4SP thymocytes exhibited unusually high Qa2 expression.
source: but a subset of Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre CD4SP thymocytes exhibited unusually high Qa2 expression (Figure 4C, top right panel).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4C show high Qa2 expression in a subset.

claim: Qa2hi CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice lacked other characteristics of maturation.
source: However, these Qa2hi CD4SP thymocytes lacked other characteristics of maturation; for example, substantial numbers of thymocytes in this subset maintained high expression of CD69 and CD24 (Figure 4E) and they failed to increase CD62L expression (Figure 4F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4E-F show abnormal marker expression in Qa2hi cells.

claim: IL-7Rα expression was partially decreased in some SP thymocytes in the absence of Pak2.
source: In the absence of Pak2, IL-7Rα expression was partially decreased in some SP thymocytes, suggesting Pak2 deficiency could affect survival of CD4SP thymocytes (Figure 4D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 4D show decreased IL-7Rα expression.

claim: The percentages of dead or apoptotic cells among resting DP and semi-mature and mature CD4SP thymocytes were comparable from WT and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice immediately after harvest.
source: The percentages of dead or apoptotic cells detected among resting DP and semi-mature and mature CD4SP thymocytes were comparable from WT and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice immediately after harvest (Figure 5A) or after 1–2 hr incubation in vitro (Figure 5B).
evidence: Apoptosis data in Figure 5A-B show similar cell death rates.

claim: A twofold increase in cell death was observed in Pak2-deficient semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes when incubated in media for 24 hr.
source: However, a twofold increase in cell death was observed in Pak2-deficient semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes when incubated in media for 24 hr, whereas mature CD4SP thymocytes from both WT and Pak2-deficient mice exhibited minimal cell death (Figure 5C).
evidence: Apoptosis data in Figure 5C show increased cell death after 24 hr.

claim: Pak2 plays a key role in the maturation and maintenance of semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes, but not in survival of mature CD4SP thymocytes.
source: Our results suggest that Pak2 plays a key role in the maturation and maintenance of semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes, but not in survival of mature CD4SP thymocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the apoptosis data in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of CD62L and integrin β7 on CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre bone marrow donors was greatly decreased in bone marrow chimeras.
source: We found that expression of CD62L and integrin β7 on CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre bone marrow donors was greatly decreased.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimeras shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Down-regulation of CD69 and CD24 was not efficient in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre bone marrow donors in chimeras.
source: Moreover, down-regulation of CD69 and CD24 was not efficient, suggesting Pak2 deficiency inhibits maturation of CD4SP thymocytes via a thymocyte intrinsic mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from bone marrow chimeras shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Pak2 deficiency inhibits maturation of CD4SP thymocytes via a thymocyte intrinsic mechanism.
source: Moreover, down-regulation of CD69 and CD24 was not efficient, suggesting Pak2 deficiency inhibits maturation of CD4SP thymocytes via a thymocyte intrinsic mechanism.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from bone marrow chimera experiments showing cell-autonomous defects.

claim: CD4SP thymocytes generated from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre bone marrow donors displayed marked reduction in IL-7Rα expression in chimeras.
source: Furthermore, CD4SP thymocytes generated from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre bone marrow donors displayed marked reduction in IL-7Rα expression, suggesting that regulation of IL-7Rα by Pak2 is cell autonomous (Figure 6C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 6C show reduced IL-7Rα expression in chimeras.

claim: CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre FTOC were blocked at the semi-mature stage.
source: Similar to what we observed in Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice, CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre FTOC were blocked at the semi-mature stage (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: FTOC data in Figure 6D-E show maturation block.

claim: IL-7Rα expression was similar on DP and CD4SP thymocytes generated from WT and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre FTOCs.
source: Interestingly, IL-7Rα expression was similar on DP and CD4SP thymocytes generated from WT and Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre FTOCs (Figure 6F), suggesting that the observed defects in IL-7Rα expression in adult CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2-deficient mice did not occur in fetal development.
evidence: FTOC data in Figure 6F show similar IL-7Rα expression.

claim: Pak2 is required for transition from the semi-mature to the mature stage in fetal and adult CD4SP thymocytes.
source: We conclude that Pak2 is required for transition from the semi-mature to the mature stage in fetal and adult CD4SP thymocytes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from FTOC experiments showing maturation block even with normal IL-7Rα expression.

claim: Expression of KLF2 was greatly reduced in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: Indeed, expression of KLF2 was greatly reduced in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 7A).
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 7A show reduced KLF2 mRNA expression.

claim: S1P1 expression was markedly decreased in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: Moreover, we found that S1P1 expression was also markedly decreased (Figure 7B), suggesting that Pak2-dependent signals regulate timed egress of SP thymocytes by controlling expression of KLF2 and S1P1.
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 7B show reduced S1P1 mRNA expression.

claim: Pak2-dependent signals regulate timed egress of SP thymocytes by controlling expression of KLF2 and S1P1.
source: Moreover, we found that S1P1 expression was also markedly decreased (Figure 7B), suggesting that Pak2-dependent signals regulate timed egress of SP thymocytes by controlling expression of KLF2 and S1P1.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reduced expression of KLF2 and S1P1 in Pak2-deficient thymocytes.

claim: A reproducible decrease in KLF2 expression was observed in the semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes of Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice.
source: However, we observed a reproducible decrease in KLF2 expression in the semi-mature CD4SP thymocytes of Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice (Figure 7A, right panel), suggesting Pak2 contributes to expression of KLF2 when CD4SP thymocytes are just beginning to upregulate KLF2.
evidence: qPCR data in Figure 7A show reduced KLF2 in semi-mature cells.

claim: Most CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice did not proliferate following TCR/CD28 stimulation.
source: In contrast, most CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice including the CD24lowQa2hi subset did not proliferate following TCR/CD28 stimulation (Figure 7C).
evidence: CFSE dilution assay data in Figure 7C show lack of proliferation.

claim: Qa2hi CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice were more susceptible to cell death following stimulation.
source: In addition, the Qa2hi CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice were more susceptible to cell death following stimulation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that these cells are not functionally mature.
evidence: Apoptosis data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A show increased cell death.

claim: Functional maturity of CD4SP thymocytes depends on Pak2.
source: Together, these results indicate that functional maturity of CD4SP thymocytes depends on Pak2.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from proliferation and cell death assays.

claim: Phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236 in CD4SP thymocytes from WT mice was increased after 24 hr of stimulation.
source: Phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236 in CD4SP thymocytes from WT mice was increased after 24 hr of stimulation (Figure 7D, top panels).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 7D show increased S6 phosphorylation.

claim: Most of the CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice displayed minimal S6 phosphorylation after 24 hr of stimulation.
source: On the contrary, most of the CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice displayed minimal S6 phosphorylation.
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 7D show reduced S6 phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236 was substantially decreased in the absence of Pak2 following 2 hr of plate-bound anti-CD3 stimulation.
source: Phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236 was substantially decreased in the absence of Pak2 (Figure 7D, bottom panels).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 7D show decreased S6 phosphorylation at 2 hr.

claim: Phosphorylation of p70S6K at T389 was decreased following 30 min and 1 hr of plate-bound CD3 stimulation in the absence of Pak2.
source: Phosphorylation of p70S6K at T389 was also decreased following 30 min and 1 hr of plate-bound CD3 stimulation in the absence of Pak2 (Figure 7E).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7E show decreased p70S6K phosphorylation.

claim: Pak2 participates in mTORC1-mediated activation of p70S6K and phosphorylation of S6 following plate-bound TCR stimulation.
source: These findings demonstrate that Pak2 participates in mTORC1-mediated activation of p70S6K and phosphorylation of S6 following plate-bound TCR stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the S6 and p70S6K phosphorylation data.

claim: Nur77 induction was greatly decreased in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice following 24 hr of anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: Nur77 induction was greatly decreased in CD4SP thymocytes from Pak2F/F;Cd4-Cre mice following 24 hr of anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation (Figure 7F).
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 7F show decreased Nur77 induction.

claim: Pak2 is required for downstream events reflective of TCR signaling, including those inducing Nur77 induction and p70S6K activation.
source: These results reveal that Pak2 is required for downstream events reflective of TCR signaling, including those inducing Nur77 induction and p70S6K activation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the Nur77 and p70S6K data.

claim: Phosphorylation of Erk1/2 was markedly reduced in the absence of Pak2 when cells were stimulated by plate-bound anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: Phosphorylation of Erk1/2 was markedly reduced in the absence of Pak2, when cells were stimulated by plate-bound anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 stimulation (Figure 7G,H).
evidence: Flow cytometry and Western blot data in Figure 7G-H show reduced Erk1/2 phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of Erk1/2 was not reduced when cells were stimulated by soluble anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 in the absence of Pak2.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation of Erk1/2 was not reduced when cells were stimulated by soluble anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 in the absence of Pak2 (data not shown), suggesting that Pak2 is required for transducing signaling events that are specifically provoked by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation but notes data not shown.

claim: Pak2 is required for transducing signaling events that are specifically provoked by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
source: In contrast, phosphorylation of Erk1/2 was not reduced when cells were stimulated by soluble anti-CD3 or anti-CD3/CD28 in the absence of Pak2 (data not shown), suggesting that Pak2 is required for transducing signaling events that are specifically provoked by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of plate-bound vs soluble stimulation.

claim: Phosphorylation of PLCγ1 is profoundly decreased in the absence of Pak2 following plate-bound TCR stimulation.
source: Indeed, we found that phosphorylation of PLCγ1 that is known to be associated with its activation status (Kim et al., 1991) is profoundly decreased in the absence of Pak2, indicating that Pak2 is required for optimal PLCγ1 activation, possibly by regulating actin cytoskeletal reorganization (Figure 7H).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7H show decreased PLCγ1 phosphorylation, and the interpretation is supported by citation to Kim et al., 1991.

claim: Pak2 is required for optimal PLCγ1 activation, possibly by regulating actin cytoskeletal reorganization.
source: Indeed, we found that phosphorylation of PLCγ1 that is known to be associated with its activation status (Kim et al., 1991) is profoundly decreased in the absence of Pak2, indicating that Pak2 is required for optimal PLCγ1 activation, possibly by regulating actin cytoskeletal reorganization (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PLCγ1 phosphorylation data and knowledge about actin cytoskeleton.

claim: The amount of polymerized filamentous actin (F-actin) was greatly increased in resting Pak2-deficient CD4SP thymocytes.
source: To our surprise, the amount of polymerized filamentous actin (F-actin) was greatly increased in resting conditions (Figure 8A), suggesting processes regulating actin assembly and disassembly were disrupted in the absence of Pak2.
evidence: Flow cytometry data in Figure 8A show increased F-actin in resting cells.

claim: Processes regulating actin assembly and disassembly were disrupted in the absence of Pak2.
source: To our surprise, the amount of polymerized filamentous actin (F-actin) was greatly increased in resting conditions (Figure 8A), suggesting processes regulating actin assembly and disassembly were disrupted in the absence of Pak2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased F-actin in resting cells.

claim: Rac1 activation was consistently increased under resting conditions in Pak2-deficient thymocytes.
source: Consistent with these data, Rac1 activation was consistently increased under resting conditions (Figure 8B).
evidence: Rac1 pull-down assay data in Figure 8B show increased Rac1 activation.

claim: Pak2-deficient CD4SP thymocytes did not reorganize their actin cytoskeleton and spread when triggered by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
source: However, despite increased F-actin and activated Rac levels, Pak2-deficient CD4SP thymocytes did not reorganize their actin cytoskeleton and spread when triggered by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 8D showing impaired spreading.

claim: WT CD4SP thymocytes exhibited intense spreading at 60 min of stimulation when plated on coverslips coated with antibodies to the TCR.
source: WT CD4SP thymocytes exhibited intense spreading at 60 min of stimulation, when they were plated on the coverslips coated with antibodies to the TCR (Figure 8D, upper left and middle panels), while polarizing F-actin of the cell body towards to the contact sites (Figure 8D, upper right panel).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data in Figure 8D show cell spreading.

claim: Pak2-deficient CD4SP thymocytes displayed poor spreading at the contact sites and actin polymerization at the contact sites was markedly impaired.
source: In stark contrast, Pak2-deficient CD4SP thymocytes displayed poor spreading at the contact sites and actin polymerization at the contact sites was markedly impaired (Figure 8D, lower left and middle panels), while F-actin in the cell was not polarized towards to the contact sites (Figure 8D, lower right panel).
evidence: Confocal microscopy data in Figure 8D show impaired spreading and actin polymerization.

claim: Areas where cells spread at the contact sites were significantly reduced in the absence of Pak2.
source: As a result, areas where cells spread at the contact sites were significantly reduced in the absence of Pak2 (Figure 8C).
evidence: Quantification of spreading areas in Figure 8C shows significant reduction.

claim: Pak2 plays a vital role in regulating the actin cytoskeletal reorganization induced by TCR stimulation.
source: These findings revealed that Pak2 plays a vital role in regulating the actin cytoskeletal reorganization induced by TCR stimulation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the cell spreading and actin polymerization data.

claim: Pak2 controls multiple stages of T cell development in the thymus by governing dynamic rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton.
source: Since the integrity of dynamic actin cytoskeletal structure and actin cytoskeletal reorganization triggered by TCR engagement are fundamental for the proper signal transmission in many biological processes of T cells, we propose that Pak2 controls multiple stages of T cell development in the thymus by governing dynamic rearrangement of the actin cytoskeleton.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the actin cytoskeleton and signaling data.

claim: Pak2 is the major PAK expressed in T cells.
source: Pak2 is the major PAK expressed in T cells (Chu et al., 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chu et al., 2004.

claim: Pak2 has been implicated in T cell function.
source: Pak2 is the major PAK expressed in T cells (Chu et al., 2004) and has been implicated in T cell function (Bubeck Wardenburg et al., 1998; Yablonski et al., 1998; Phee et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Rac and Cdc42 play crucial roles in T cell development and activation.
source: Rac, Cdc42, and Vav play crucial roles in T cell development and activation.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citations to studies on Rac, Cdc42, and Vav knockout mice.

claim: Mice lacking both isoforms of Rac1 and Rac2 show defects in pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection and T cell activation.
source: For example, mice lack both isoforms of Rac1 and Rac2 or mice deficient in Vav1 show defects in pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection and T cell activation (Turner et al., 1997; Fujikawa et al., 2003; Guo et al., 2008; Dumont et al., 2009; Tybulewicz and Henderson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mice deficient in Vav1 show defects in pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection and T cell activation.
source: For example, mice lack both isoforms of Rac1 and Rac2 or mice deficient in Vav1 show defects in pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection and T cell activation (Turner et al., 1997; Fujikawa et al., 2003; Guo et al., 2008; Dumont et al., 2009; Tybulewicz and Henderson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cdc42-deficient mice display impaired positive selection and homeostasis of T cells.
source: Cdc42-deficient mice display impaired positive selection and homeostasis of T cells (Guo et al., 2010, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guo et al., 2010, 2011.

claim: The P21-activated kinases (PAKs) are effector molecules of Rac and Cdc42.
source: The p21-activated kinases (PAKs), effector molecules of Rac and Cdc42, participate in diverse cellular signaling pathways including cell spreading, adhesion, migration, activation, proliferation, and survival (Manser et al., 1994; Bokoch, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manser et al., 1994 and Bokoch, 2003.

claim: PAKs participate in diverse cellular signaling pathways including cell spreading, adhesion, migration, activation, proliferation, and survival.
source: The p21-activated kinases (PAKs), effector molecules of Rac and Cdc42, participate in diverse cellular signaling pathways including cell spreading, adhesion, migration, activation, proliferation, and survival (Manser et al., 1994; Bokoch, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Manser et al., 1994 and Bokoch, 2003.

claim: PAKs are serine/threonine kinases that phosphorylate multiple substrates.
source: PAKs are serine/threonine kinases that phosphorylate multiple substrates, including those that are involved in cytoskeletal reorganization, cell proliferation, and survival.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PAK kinases.

claim: The group I PAK family consists of three kinases (Pak1, Pak2 and Pak3).
source: The group I PAK family consists of three kinases (Pak1, Pak2 and Pak3) (Bokoch, 2003; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bokoch, 2003 and Kelly and Chernoff, 2012.

claim: Pak2 knock-out mice exhibit embryonic lethality.
source: However, the in vivo role of Pak2 in T cells is not known due to embryonic lethality of Pak2 knock-out (KO) mice (Hofmann et al., 2004; Kelly and Chernoff, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hofmann et al., 2004 and Kelly and Chernoff, 2012.

claim: Pak2 is required for the development, maturation, and timed egress of thymocytes.
source: In this study, we show for the first time that Pak2 is required for the development, maturation, and timed egress of thymocytes.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Lineage-specific deletion of Pak2 at an early T cell developmental stage using the Lck-Cre impaired pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection similar to the mice that lack Rac1/2 or Vav1.
source: Lineage-specific deletion of Pak2 at an early T cell developmental stage using the Lck-Cre impaired pre-TCR β-selection and positive selection similar to the mice that lack Rac1/2 or Vav1.
evidence: This is a summary of findings comparing Pak2 deletion to Rac1/2 or Vav1 deletion.

claim: Deletion of Pak2 at a later developmental stage using the Cd4-Cre severely inhibited functional maturation of CD4SP thymocytes.
source: Surprisingly, deletion of Pak2 at a later developmental stage using the Cd4-Cre severely inhibited functional maturation of CD4SP thymocytes, including impaired expression of S1P1 accompanied by reduced expression of its transcription factor, KLF2.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Cd4-Cre deletion experiments.

claim: TCR-mediated signaling was greatly decreased in the absence of Pak2, including Nur77 induction and S6 phosphorylation.
source: TCR-mediated signaling was greatly decreased in the absence of Pak2, including Nur77 induction and S6 phosphorylation, leading to decreased proliferation.
evidence: This is a summary of signaling defects observed in Pak2-deficient cells.

claim: Pak2 deficiency impaired actin cytoskeletal remodeling and activation of PLCγ1 and Erk1/2 triggered by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
source: Mechanistically, Pak2 deficiency impaired actin cytoskeletal remodeling and activation of PLCγ1 and Erk1/2 triggered by plate-bound TCR stimulation.
evidence: This is a summary of mechanistic findings.

claim: Pak2 is an essential regulator that drives the actin cytoskeleton-dependent signaling for normal thymocyte development and maturation.
source: These findings reveal a critical function of Pak2 as an essential regulator that drives the actin cytoskeleton-dependent signaling for normal thymocyte development and maturation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Signals that result from successful TCR β-chain rearrangement and a pre-TCR formation drive the most immature CD4 and CD8 double negative (DN) thymocytes to become CD4 and CD8 double positive (DP), known as β-selection.
source: Signals that result from successful TCR β-chain rearrangement and a pre-TCR formation drive the most immature CD4 and CD8 double negative (DN) thymocytes to become CD4 and CD8 double positive (DP), known as β-selection (Mallick et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mallick et al., 1993.

claim: Following TCR α-chain rearrangement and mature TCR expression, DP thymocytes undergo positive selection using their newly assembled TCRs to recognize self peptide-major histocompatibility (pMHC) proteins expressed by the cTECs.
source: Following TCR α-chain rearrangement and mature TCR expression, DP thymocytes undergo positive selection using their newly assembled TCRs to recognize self peptide-major histocompatibility (pMHC) proteins expressed by the cTECs (cortical thymic epithelial cells).
evidence: This is established knowledge about thymocyte development.

claim: A small number of DP thymocytes successfully undergo positive selection and ultimately mature into CD4 or CD8 single positive (SP) cells.
source: A small number of DP thymocytes successfully undergo positive selection and ultimately mature into CD4 or CD8 single positive (SP) cells (Scollay and Shortman, 1985; Petrie et al., 1990; Starr et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Fully mature SP thymocytes become competent to proliferate when stimulated via their TCR, in contrast to DP or semi-mature SP thymocytes that are subject to apoptosis.
source: Fully mature SP thymocytes become competent to proliferate, when stimulated via their TCR, in contrast to DP or semi-mature SP thymocytes that are subject to apoptosis (Hogquist et al., 2005; Takada et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hogquist et al., 2005 and Takada et al., 2011.

claim: Post-positive selection DP and SP thymocytes increase their IL-7R expression to promote their survival.
source: Moreover, post-positive selection DP and SP thymocytes increase their IL-7R expression to promote their survival (Van De Wiele et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van De Wiele et al., 2004 and Yu et al., 2006.

claim: As SP thymocytes mature, they decrease expression of CD69 and CD24 and concurrently increase expression of CD62L and Qa2.
source: As SP thymocytes mature, they decrease expression of CD69 and CD24 and concurrently increase expression of CD62L and Qa2 (Vernachio et al., 1989; Ramsdell et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vernachio et al., 1989 and Ramsdell et al., 1991.

claim: Only functionally mature T cells exit the thymus, which is enabled, in part, by the marked increase in expression of egress receptors, including sphingosine 1 phosphate receptor 1 (S1P1).
source: Only functionally mature T cells exit the thymus, which is enabled, in part, by the marked increase in expression of egress receptors, including sphingosine 1 phosphate receptor 1 (S1P1) (Allende et al., 2004; Matloubian et al., 2004; Weinreich and Hogquist, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: The transcription factor Kruppel Lung Factor 2 (KLF2) controls expression of S1P1 and CD62L.
source: The transcription factor Kruppel Lung Factor 2 (KLF2) controls expression of S1P1 and CD62L (Carlson et al., 2006; Weinreich and Hogquist, 2008), thereby governing egress of T cells from the thymus and facilitating entry to the lymph nodes.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Carlson et al., 2006 and Weinreich and Hogquist, 2008.

claim: KLF2 governs egress of T cells from the thymus and facilitates entry to the lymph nodes.
source: The transcription factor Kruppel Lung Factor 2 (KLF2) controls expression of S1P1 and CD62L (Carlson et al., 2006; Weinreich and Hogquist, 2008), thereby governing egress of T cells from the thymus and facilitating entry to the lymph nodes.
evidence: This is an inference based on KLF2's control of S1P1 and CD62L expression.

claim: TCR engagement drastically induces changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture and reorganizes it.
source: TCR engagement drastically induces changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture and reorganizes it.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR signaling.

claim: Actin cytoskeletal reorganization influences T cell signaling leading to T cell activation.
source: Actin cytoskeletal reorganization influences T cell signaling leading to T cell activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the role of actin cytoskeleton in T cell signaling.

claim: TCR-mediated actin polymerization is required to form extensive contacts between T cells and antigen presenting cells (APCs), organize gross cell polarity, and stabilize signaling complexes acting as a scaffold for further assembly.
source: For instance, TCR-mediated actin polymerization is required to form extensive contacts between T cells and antigen presenting cells (APCs), organize gross cell polarity, and stabilize signaling complexes acting as a scaffold for further assembly (Wülfing and Davis, 1998; Kaizuka et al., 2007; Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Rho family GTPases such as Rac and Cdc42 regulate cytoskeletal reorganization, microtubule dynamics, and cell polarity in many cell types, including T cells.
source: Rho family GTPases such as Rac and Cdc42 regulate cytoskeletal reorganization, microtubule dynamics, and cell polarity in many cell types, including T cells (Zhao and Manser, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Zhao and Manser, 2005.

claim: Activation of Rho family GTPases is tightly regulated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs).
source: Activation of Rho family GTPases is tightly regulated by guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) (Tybulewicz and Henderson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tybulewicz and Henderson, 2009.

claim: Vav family proteins (Vav1, Vav2 and Vav3) are GEFs for Rac and Cdc42.
source: Vav family proteins (Vav1, Vav2 and Vav3) are GEFs for Rac and Cdc42 (Tybulewicz, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Tybulewicz, 2005.

claim: Activation of PLCγ1 plays a critical role in activating Erk1/2 following TCR stimulation.
source: Since activation of PLCγ1 plays a critical role in activating Erk1/2 following TCR stimulation, we hypothesized that Pak2 participates in activation of Erk1/2 via promoting PLCγ1 activation by regulating actin cytoskeletal dynamics during T cell spreading triggered by TCR engagement.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TCR signaling pathways.

claim: Actin dynamics that mediate ongoing actin polymerization and retrograde flow promotes sustained PLCγ1 signaling during plate-bound TCR activation.
source: Interestingly, actin dynamics that mediate ongoing actin polymerization and retrograde flow promotes sustained PLCγ1 signaling during plate-bound TCR activation, while disruption of F-actin dynamics inhibits sustained PLCγ1 phosphorylation (Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Babich et al., 2012.

claim: Disruption of F-actin dynamics inhibits sustained PLCγ1 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, actin dynamics that mediate ongoing actin polymerization and retrograde flow promotes sustained PLCγ1 signaling during plate-bound TCR activation, while disruption of F-actin dynamics inhibits sustained PLCγ1 phosphorylation (Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Babich et al., 2012.

claim: Activation of PLCγ1 and Ras-mediated MAPK pathway leading to Erk1/2 activation are essential for positive selection.
source: Activation of PLCγ1 (Sommers et al., 2005; Fu et al., 2010) and Ras-mediated MAPK pathway leading to Erk1/2 activation are essential for positive selection (Alberola-Ila et al., 1995; Swan et al., 1995; O'Shea et al., 1996; Swat et al., 1996; Pagès et al., 1999; Fischer et al., 2005; McGargill et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Positive selection is initiated by TCR/pMHC interaction between DP thymocytes and cTECs and controlled by avidity and affinity of this interaction.
source: Since positive selection is initiated by TCR/pMHC interaction between DP thymocytes and cTECs and controlled by avidity and affinity of this interaction (Starr et al., 2003), inefficient signaling such as impaired activation of PLCγ1 and Erk1/2 could lead to defects in positive selection in the absence of Pak2.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Starr et al., 2003.

claim: Inefficient signaling such as impaired activation of PLCγ1 and Erk1/2 could lead to defects in positive selection in the absence of Pak2.
source: Since positive selection is initiated by TCR/pMHC interaction between DP thymocytes and cTECs and controlled by avidity and affinity of this interaction (Starr et al., 2003), inefficient signaling such as impaired activation of PLCγ1 and Erk1/2 could lead to defects in positive selection in the absence of Pak2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the signaling defects observed in Pak2-deficient cells.

claim: Disruption of actin dynamics by administration of either the F-actin stabilizing agent jasplakinolide or the actin depolymerizing agent latrunculin completely abrogated signaling events such as induction of Nur77 and S6 phosphorylation following plate-bound TCR stimulation.
source: We also confirmed that disruption of actin dynamics by administration of either the F-actin stabilizing agent jasplakinolide (Bubb et al., 1994; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005) or the actin depolymerizing agent latrunculin (Spector et al., 1983; Coué et al., 1987) completely abrogated signaling events such as induction of Nur77 and S6 phosphorylation following plate-bound TCR stimulation (data not shown), suggesting actin cytoskeletal reorganization is critical for activation of TCR-induced signaling events.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation but notes data not shown, and cites references for the agents used.

claim: Actin cytoskeletal reorganization is critical for activation of TCR-induced signaling events.
source: We also confirmed that disruption of actin dynamics by administration of either the F-actin stabilizing agent jasplakinolide (Bubb et al., 1994; Murthy and Wadsworth, 2005) or the actin depolymerizing agent latrunculin (Spector et al., 1983; Coué et al., 1987) completely abrogated signaling events such as induction of Nur77 and S6 phosphorylation following plate-bound TCR stimulation (data not shown), suggesting actin cytoskeletal reorganization is critical for activation of TCR-induced signaling events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the effects of actin-disrupting agents.

claim: Post-positive selection DP thymocytes migrate from the thymic cortex to the medulla and spend about 4–5 days there prior to exiting.
source: After completing positive selection, post-positive selection DP thymocytes migrate from the thymic cortex to the medulla and spend about 4–5 days there prior to exiting (McCaughtry et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughtry et al., 2007.

claim: Newly selected SP thymocytes acquire 'mature' features in the medulla before they egress.
source: Newly selected SP thymocytes acquire 'mature' features in the medulla before they egress (McCaughtry et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughtry et al., 2007.

claim: KLF2 does not contribute to functional maturation of thymocytes because KLF2-deficient SP thymocytes are not defective in proliferation following CD3/CD28 stimulation.
source: Although KLF2 plays a critical role in egress and trafficking, KLF2 does not contribute to functional maturation of thymocytes because KLF2-deficient SP thymocytes are not defective in proliferation following CD3/CD28 stimulation (Takada et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Takada et al., 2011.

claim: Pak2 plays essential roles in promoting functional maturation as well as KLF2 expression.
source: On the other hand, Pak2 plays essential roles in promoting functional maturation as well as KLF2 expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing both functional maturation defects and reduced KLF2 expression.

claim: Pak2-mediated functional maturation is required for the increased expression of KLF2.
source: These results indicate that Pak2-mediated functional maturation is required for the increased expression of KLF2.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that Pak2 is required for both functional maturation and KLF2 expression.

claim: Timed egress of thymocytes by KLF2 is tightly coordinated by a Pak2-dependent maturation process as a quality checkpoint mechanism.
source: We propose that timed egress of thymocytes by KLF2 is tightly coordinated by a Pak2-dependent maturation process as a quality checkpoint mechanism.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings.

claim: Cd4-Cre mediated Pak2 deletion results in severe T cell lymphopenia due to Pak2's multiple roles in T cell maturation and timed egress of thymocytes.
source: As a consequence, Cd4-Cre mediated Pak2 deletion results in severe T cell lymphopenia due to Pak2's multiple roles in T cell maturation and timed egress of thymocytes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the multiple defects observed in Pak2-deficient mice.

claim: Pak2 may regulate thymic development by controlling TCR-mediated signaling strength by facilitating actin cytoskeletal reorganization.
source: Therefore, Pak2 may regulate thymic development by controlling TCR-mediated signaling strength by facilitating actin cytoskeletal reorganization.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the findings.

claim: Pak2 is required for thymic development, including pre-TCR β selection and positive selection, and T cell activation, closely resembling the functions of Rac, Cdc42 or their activator Vav in T cell development and activation.
source: Here, we show that Pak2 is required for thymic development, including pre-TCR β selection and positive selection, and T cell activation, closely resembling the functions of Rac, Cdc42 or their activator Vav in T cell development and activation.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion comparing Pak2 function to Rac, Cdc42, and Vav.

claim: Pak2 is the primary effector for mediating the functions of Rac and Cdc42 in T cell development and activation.
source: Together, our findings suggest that Pak2 is the primary effector for mediating the functions of Rac and Cdc42 in T cell development and activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the similarity of phenotypes between Pak2-deficient and Rac/Cdc42-deficient mice.

claim: Phosphorylation of S6 at the S235/S236 sites and p70S6K at the T389 site were completely abrogated by rapamycin.
source: Activation of mTORC1 pathway was absolutely required for phosphorylation of S6 at the S235/S236 sites and p70S6K at the T389 site, as phosphorylation of these sites were completely abrogated by rapamycin, an inhibitor of mTOR (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B-E show complete inhibition by rapamycin.

claim: Treatment of thymocytes with a MEK inhibitor, UO126, partially reduced phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236.
source: Indeed, treatment of thymocytes with a MEK inhibitor, UO126, partially reduced phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236 (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-E show partial reduction.

claim: Rapamycin treatment completely abrogated phosphorylation of S6 at S235/S236.
source: However, since rapamycin treatment completely abrogated phosphorylation of S6 at these sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–E), the MAPK-dependent phosphorylation of S6 also seems to depend on activation of mTORC1-mediated pathway.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-E show complete inhibition by rapamycin.

claim: The MAPK-dependent phosphorylation of S6 depends on activation of mTORC1-mediated pathway.
source: However, since rapamycin treatment completely abrogated phosphorylation of S6 at these sites (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–E), the MAPK-dependent phosphorylation of S6 also seems to depend on activation of mTORC1-mediated pathway.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rapamycin inhibition data.

claim: Phosphorylation of p70S6K at T389 was completely dependent upon mTOR-mediated pathway but independent of MAPK-mediated pathway.
source: To determine whether reduced phosphorylation of S6 in the absence of Pak2 is due to inhibition of mTORC1-mediated pathway, we examined phosphorylation of p70S6K at the T389 site because phosphorylation of this site was completely dependent on mTORC1-mediated pathway but independent of MAPK-mediated pathway (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C–E).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C-E show pathway dependencies.

claim: TCR engagement by plating T cells on surfaces coated with antibodies to the TCR mimics T cell activation by antigen-presenting cells (APCs).
source: TCR engagement by plating T cells on surfaces coated with antibodies to the TCR mimics T cell activation by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and triggers dynamic changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture, such as formation and expansion of contacts bounded by continuously remodeled actin-rich rings (Wear et al., 2000; Bunnell et al., 2001; Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Plate-bound TCR stimulation triggers dynamic changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture, such as formation and expansion of contacts bounded by continuously remodeled actin-rich rings.
source: TCR engagement by plating T cells on surfaces coated with antibodies to the TCR mimics T cell activation by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) and triggers dynamic changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture, such as formation and expansion of contacts bounded by continuously remodeled actin-rich rings (Wear et al., 2000; Bunnell et al., 2001; Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: Actin-rich rings are associated with extension of lamellipodia that requires assembly and disassembly of actin filament networks.
source: These actin-rich rings are associated with extension of lamellipodia that requires assembly and disassembly of actin filament neworks (Bunnell et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bunnell et al., 2001.

claim: Changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture induced by TCR engagement promote T cell signaling.
source: Changes in actin cytoskeletal architecture induced by TCR engagement promote T cell signaling (Babich et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Babich et al., 2012.

claim: The PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 signaling pathway has been reported to be activated by the TCR and CD28 stimulation, reflected in the phosphorylation of S6 ribosomal protein (S6).
source: The PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 signaling pathway has been reported to be activated by the TCR and CD28 stimulation, reflected in the phosphorylation of S6 ribosomal protein (S6), a direct target of the mTORC1-activated p70S6 kinase (p70S6K) (Hay and Sonenberg, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hay and Sonenberg, 2004.

claim: S6 is a direct target of the mTORC1-activated p70S6 kinase (p70S6K).
source: The PI3K/Akt/mTORC1 signaling pathway has been reported to be activated by the TCR and CD28 stimulation, reflected in the phosphorylation of S6 ribosomal protein (S6), a direct target of the mTORC1-activated p70S6 kinase (p70S6K) (Hay and Sonenberg, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hay and Sonenberg, 2004.

claim: Activation of the mTORC1 pathway increases rates of mRNA translation and protein synthesis, which permits increased cell growth and proliferation.
source: Activation of the mTORC1 pathway increases rates of mRNA translation and protein synthesis, which permits increased cell growth and proliferation (Mills and Jameson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mills and Jameson, 2009.

claim: TCR-induced S6 phosphorylation reaches its optimal amounts after 1 or 2 hr of TCR stimulation and lasts up to 5 hr.
source: Since TCR-induced S6 phosphorylation reaches its optimal amounts after 1 or 2 hr of TCR stimulation and lasts up to 5 hr (Salmond et al., 2009; van den Brink et al., 1999), we examined S6 phosphorylation following 2 hr of plate-bound anti-CD3 stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Salmond et al., 2009 and van den Brink et al., 1999.

claim: Activation of MAPK-RSK pathway contributes to phosphorylation of S6.
source: Activation of MAPK-RSK pathway contributes to phosphorylation of S6 (Salmond et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Salmond et al., 2009.

claim: Nur77 is an orphan nuclear hormone receptor induced in response to TCR stimulation, as a reporter for TCR strength of signaling.
source: To determine whether Pak2-deficient CD4SP thymocytes have a defect in optimal activation of integrated TCR-mediated signaling events, we examined expression of Nur77, an orphan nuclear hormone receptor induced in response to TCR stimulation, as a reporter for TCR strength of signaling (Moran et al., 2011; Zikherman et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moran et al., 2011 and Zikherman et al., 2012.

claim: Activation of Erk1/2 following TCR stimulation plays a key role in thymic development as well as in induction of Nur77.
source: Because activation of Erk1/2 following TCR stimulation plays a key role in thymic development as well as in induction of Nur77 (van den Brink et al., 1999), we examined activation of Erk1/2 following TCR or TCR/CD28 stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to van den Brink et al., 1999.

claim: Phosphorylation of PLCγ1 is known to be associated with its activation status.
source: Indeed, we found that phosphorylation of PLCγ1 that is known to be associated with its activation status (Kim et al., 1991) is profoundly decreased in the absence of Pak2
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kim et al., 1991.

claim: CD5 expression is indicative of basal TCR signaling.
source: In addition, the expression of CD5 was markedly lower in DP and CD4SP thymocytes (Figure 2I) with a reduced percentage of post-positive selection cells (data not shown) from OTII+;Pak2F/F;Lck-Cre mice, indicative of lower basal TCR signaling (Azzam et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Azzam et al., 1998.
